module_title: Foundation Model Customization, Evaluation and Bedrock Applications
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 21 through 24 individually, including guardrail filters, order lookup examples, OpenAPI parameters, Lambda action execution and traces; concise visual-first narration reviewed.

scenes.title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
scenes.narration: This slide shows where Amazon Bedrock Guardrails fit around a generative AI request. Follow the five boxes across the top. A user submits a prompt; configured input checks inspect it before it reaches a supported foundation model. The model generates a reply, then configured output checks assess that response before the application returns it. The lower row lists five controls. Content filtering can detect harmful categories; topic restrictions limit disallowed subjects; word filters target specified words or phrases. Sensitive-information filtering can block or mask supported personal data, like the email address shown here. Contextual grounding checks, where supported, help detect answers unsupported by supplied documents. These are configurable policies, not perfect guarantees. Consider a customer-support chatbot: it might need to mask personal contact details while still answering a valid billing question. Finally, see the lock icon at the bottom. Guardrails do not replace IAM permissions or authorization in your application. Test policies against realistic prompts, monitor interventions, and make sure the user is allowed to access the underlying data.

scenes.title: Amazon Bedrock Agents: coordinate tasks
scenes.narration: Here the customer asks, 'Where is my order?' Follow the five stages. The Bedrock agent uses its instructions, selected model and conversation history to decide the next step. Because the order ID is missing, it asks the customer to provide it. The example customer replies with A1234567. The agent then invokes the configured Order Lookup action group, which securely reads the order system. The result is returned to the agent, which tells the customer that the order is on its way and expected tomorrow. This is more than ordinary text generation: the agent coordinates a real backend lookup. The purple Knowledge Base panel at the bottom shows an optional source for shipping or return policies, distinct from live order status. The blue permissions panel is crucial. An agent may only use the tools and backend permissions explicitly configured for it. It cannot assume permission to place orders, change accounts, or perform arbitrary infrastructure actions. Choose agents when a task needs controlled steps and tools, not just a single answer from a model.

scenes.title: Action groups and tool contracts
scenes.narration: This slide opens up the action group from the order example. Start with the left panel. An OpenAPI schema or function definition describes an operation called getOrderStatus and requires an orderId string. The code also shows an HTTP GET operation, a query parameter and a successful response description. This is a contract explaining what information the tool expects; it does not grant access by itself. In the next panel, the customer asks for an order status without supplying the ID. The agent checks the required parameter and asks for it. Once the user provides ORD-12345, the configured backend in the third panel executes getOrderStatus with that value. Here AWS Lambda performs a read-only order database lookup and returns the result. The final panel shows the agent reporting that ORD-12345 is Shipped, along with the illustrative delivery date. Notice that this example only reads status; it does not place an order. A safe implementation still needs identity checks, permission enforcement and validation inside the backend. Defining a function name is not the same as authorizing its execution.

scenes.title: Agent reasoning and tool-use workflow
scenes.narration: This diagram shows the full tool-use cycle. The customer asks for order number 12345, so the agent first checks that the required order number is present. In the third panel it chooses OrderStatusTool from the configured options, rather than KnowledgeSearchTool or CustomerSupportTool. The selected tool runs through an authorized Lambda or other backend, which reads the order database. Next the agent examines the tool result and decides whether it has enough information. The diamond labeled 'Enough information?' can lead to another supported lookup, such as retrieving policy context from a Knowledge Base. If the order result is sufficient, the agent gives the sourced response shown below: the order is shipped and expected tomorrow, with OrderStatusTool identified as the source. Follow the trace along the bottom: request, interpretation, tool selection, execution, result and response. These high-level orchestration events help diagnose failures without exposing a model's private internal reasoning. For troubleshooting, inspect the selected tool, inputs, permissions, outputs and whether another lookup was necessary.
